question_en: An analyst has collected the following data for a noncallable, nonconvertible preferred stock: Based on this information, the stock is most likely:
explanation_en: Regarding shareholder wealth, all else being equal, repurchasing shares is comparable to paying cash dividends; both return cash to shareholders. A share repurchase allows the company greater control in the timing and size of shareholder distributions. Some companies prefer this approach to avoid a regular cash dividend and all the market expectations that go along with paying it. By controlling the timing and size of share repurchase, management can buy shares to support the share price and/or offset the exercise of employee stock options. Share repurchase has also gained popularity since it is often a more tax-efficient means of returning cash to shareholders. Repurchased shares are excluded from the earnings per share (EPS) calculation. This has a positive impact on EPS growth and is also a reason why a company's management pursues share repurchase instead of a cash dividend. (Choices A and C) Shares that have been repurchased are not eligible to participate in cash dividends or shareholder voting.

question_en: In valuing equities, a disadvantage of using the method of comparables with price multiples is most likely that it:
option_b: does not work well for industry analysis.
option_c: is impacted by choice of accounting methods.
explanation_en: Analysts most commonly use the method of comparables (comps) to compare and report on price multiples. The analyst compares the price multiple of a company stock to that of a benchmark (ie, similar company stock or industry average). If the price multiple of the stock is lower than the benchmark, then the stock is considered to be undervalued, the same as the benchmark, then the stock is considered to be fairly valued, higher than the benchmark, then the stock is considered to be overvalued. Comps can be used in two ways. Cross-sectional analysis involves comparing the price multiples of different assets to each other over the same time period. Time-series analysis involves comparing the average price multiple of a single asset over multiple time periods. Since time series analysis is used in this scenario, the average price multiple of the stock itself over time is the benchmark. When the benchmark is an industry average price multiple or that of a similar stock, it is more likely that cross-sectional analysis is being used (Choices A and C).

question_en: An advantage of using the justified forward P/E ratio in valuation of a company's equity is that it most likely:
option_a: provides a way to compare companies in the future.
option_b: does not require estimating future company values or cash flows.
option_c: can be reliably compared to trailing price multiples of other companies.
explanation_en:
Price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios
Trailing P/E Forward P/E Justified forward P/E
Justified by future flows
Numerator Current price
(free cash flow, dividends)
Denominator Past earnings Future earnings Future earnings
A price multiple is the ratio of a company's stock price to another fundamental value or cash flow. One such multiple is the price-to-earnings ratio
(P/E ratio), which is equal to the company's stock price divided by its earnings per share. For example, if a company's earnings per share is CNY
2 and the stock price is CNY 40, the P/E ratio is 40 / 2 = 20.
The P/E ratio is used in mainly three different forms: trailing P/E, forward P/E ratio (ie, prospective or leading P/E), and justified forward P/E.
Trailing P/E uses past earnings. An obvious drawback of using trailing P/E is that it fails to consider a company's future earnings.
Forward P/E is based on future earnings. If the forward P/E ratio estimate is based on a model of future company fundamentals or cash flows, the
ratio is referred to as justified forward P/E. Using a justified forward multiple allows comparison of company price multiples in the future.
(Choice B) Justified forward P/E requires estimating future earnings growth using a predictive model, such as the Gordon growth model.
(Choice C) Justified forward P/E is based on an estimate of future earnings, whereas trailing P/E is based on past or recent earnings. For this
reason, the leading P/E of one company should not be compared with the trailing P/E of another company, as this will produce misleading
conclusions.

question_en: When estimating a company's intrinsic value using an asset-based valuation model, an analyst would least likely need the value of the company's:
explanation_en:
Asset-based valuation models
An asset-based valuation model estimates a company's value as the common shareholders' claim on the company's net assets. These models
calculate the company's value as:
the market value of its assets, less
the market value of its liabilities and
the value of its preferred shares.
These market values include any off–balance sheet items that have value. The value of preferred shares must be removed from net assets in
asset-based models since preferred shareholders' claims have priority over those of common shareholders (Choice B).
Capital expenditures are a cash flow item measuring the value of new fixed assets a company has purchased during a period. Capital
expenditures increase the company's assets but are not needed for asset-based valuation models since their value will already be reflected in
the company's assets. Similarly, any debt required to fund the purchase of capital expenditures would be reflected in the company's liabilities.
(Choice A) The value of liabilities is needed in asset-based valuation models since liabilities are subtracted from assets to calculate the net value
of the assets.

question_en: An analyst uses the method of comparables to evaluate cyclical companies during economic downturns. Which of the following ratios is least likely to be useful for that analysis?
explanation_en:
Multiples based on price and enterprise value are widely used to assess the relative value of comparable companies [ie, method of
comparables]. Such multiplier models are attractive since their factors are easy to obtain and the process is much less complicated than valuation
methods that attempt to estimate intrinsic value (eg, discounted cash flow analysis).
Companies are usually valued based on their long-term prospects. However, typical valuation multiples use operating measures (eg, earnings,
EBITDA) for a single year. In economic downturns, the earnings of companies in cyclical industries are often highly depressed or negative (ie, net
losses). Negative earnings result in negative P/E ratios, which are problematic due to the difficulty of interpreting their meaning for relative
value.
(Choices A and C) Although the sales and EBITDA of cyclical companies are also depressed during economic downturns, both measures are
likely to remain positive. Therefore, analysts are not confronted with the problem of interpreting a negative ratio when using price-to-sales or
enterprise value-to-EBITDA.

subtopic: 6.08 Equity Valuation Concepts And Basic Tools
question_en: Which of the following is most likely the rationale for using the method of comparables to value equities?
explanation_en:
The most common way analysts compare and report on price multiples is the method of comparables. An analyst compares the price multiple of a
company stock to a benchmark (ie, price multiple of a similar company stock or average). In a well-functioning financial system, arbitrage forces
identical assets to have the same price. Therefore, a price multiple should be close to its benchmark.
Market participants engage in arbitrage by purchasing a lower-priced asset and selling it at a higher price. This puts upward pressure on the lower
price and downward pressure on the higher price until the prices of the identical assets converge. The method of comparables is based on the
law of one price, which is enforced by arbitrage.
(Choice A) The present value approach assumes that an asset's intrinsic value is equal to the discounted value of all its future cash flows and
then compares that value to the asset's market price to determine whether it is fairly priced. In contrast, the method of comparables measures an
asset's price against a benchmark of similar assets.
(Choice C) Competitive advantage is a set of business conditions or company attributes that allows a business to outperform competitors and
achieve superior results. Competitive advantage may allow one firm to sell at a lower price than its competitors but would not be associated with
identical assets having the same price.

question_en: To estimate a company's intrinsic value using a present value model, an analyst most likely needs to estimate the:
option_c: cash flows available to common shareholders.
explanation_en:
Each type of equity valuation model uses different metrics to estimate intrinsic value. Present value (ie, discounted cash flow [DCF]) equity
valuation models estimate value from the projected future cash flows accruing to the benefit of common shareholders. These models use
either cash distributions (ie, dividends) or cash available to distribute (ie, free cash flow to equity). Intrinsic value estimates from these models are
the present value of the appropriate cash flow.
(Choice A) Asset-based models value equities using the estimated fair market value of a company's assets and liabilities.
(Choice B) Multiplier models determine valuation relative to the same price multiple (eg, P/E ratios) for comparable companies.

question_en: When using present value models for valuing nondividend-paying stocks, which of the following should analysts most appropriately discount?
explanation_en:
Present value models, also called discounted cash flow (DCF) models, estimate equity values using projected cash flows accruing to the
benefit of stockholders. There are two categories of present value models, each using a different proxy for cash flows:
Dividend discount models (DDM) use projected dividend distributions.
Free-cash-flow-to-equity (FCFE) models use the forecasts of cash available for distribution.
If a company does not pay a dividend, it is difficult to apply a DDM. However, a company's operating history provides a basis for projecting its
ability to generate free cash flow. Thus, FCFE models are more commonly used to value nondividend-paying stocks.
(Choice A) Projected operating cash flows are usually a major component, but not the entirety, of free cash flow, and so are not as appropriate as
a proxy. Often referred to as cash flow from operations (CFO), these amounts require adjustments for debt retirement and issuance, changes in
working capital requirements, and investment in fixed assets when projecting FCFE.
(Choice C) Earnings available to common shareholders are the earnings used in P/E multiplier models. Earnings are not used in present value
models since earnings are not fully realized in cash but are based on accounting revenues and expenses.

question_en: An analyst estimates a firm's enterprise value (EV) using an EV/EBITDA multiple and then correctly calculates the firm's implied equity value from its EV. If the equity value is higher than the EV, the most likely reason is that:
option_b: the firm's stock is greatly undervalued.
option_c: the firm has more cash than debt and preferred stock.
explanation_en:
To estimate a firm's enterprise value (EV), analysts often multiply the firm's EBITDA by an EV/EBITDA ratio. Enterprise value measures the value
of a firm's operations, which is supported by equity and nonequity sources of capital.
Equity value measures the value to common shareholders.
Nonequity claims, or net debt, measure the value to other providers of capital, such as preferred shareholders and creditors.
Note: Net debt is net of cash since cash can be used to pay down debt.
Theoretically, equity value is what owners would receive from selling a business after settling net debt. In some cases (such as this scenario),
equity value can exceed enterprise value due to negative net debt: The firm has more cash and marketable investments than its gross
nonequity claims (eg, debt, preferred stock, noncontrolling interest).
(Choice A) A low EV/EBITDA multiple has no impact on net debt. Therefore, a low EV/EBITDA multiple does not contribute to the difference
between EV and equity value.
(Choice B) A judgment about the firm's stock valuation compares its estimated intrinsic equity value to its market equity value, not to an estimated
EV.

question_en: The free cash flow to equity model most likely focuses on a firm's capacity to:
explanation_en:
Present value models base the equity value of a firm on its projected future cash flows. These models derive intrinsic value by discounting a firm's
future cash flows (eg, free cash flow to equity, dividends).
Free cash flow to equity (FCFE) represents the remaining cash available to shareholders after making investments in working capital, fixed
capital (ie, PPE), and servicing debt. Companies can use FCFE to pay dividends to shareholders or buy back shares; therefore, the value of
shareholder's equity can be derived using FCFE. This valuation model emphasizes a firm's capacity (ie, ability) to pay dividends.
Alternatively, the dividend discount model (DDM) is sometimes used to estimate the value of equity by using expected dividend payments as cash
flow inputs. This may be used for companies that have a stable record for paying dividends.
(Choice A) FCFE represents cash available only to equity investors, not to debtholders. Free cash flow to the firm (FCFF) is cash flow available
to all capital (ie, debt and equity) providers. FCFE equals FCFF minus debt payments.
(Choice C) FCFE is calculated from cash generated by business activities (ie, cash from operations) after accounting for investments in fixed
capital. Therefore, investments in fixed capital are not made from FCFE.

question_en: A company has a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) of 5. In reviewing the company's financial data, an analyst estimates a justified forward P/E of 4. Based on the justified forward P/E, the stock is:
explanation_en:
The price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio is the company's stock price as a multiple of its earnings per share.
A forward P/E ratio is based on the observed market price and a forward earnings estimate.
A justified forward P/E ratio is based on an intrinsic value for price and a forward earnings estimate.
The justified forward P/E ratio can be compared with other forms of the P/E ratio to determine whether a stock is mispriced. If the justified
forward P/E based on intrinsic value is less (greater) than the forward P/E based on market value, the stock is considered overvalued
(undervalued) by the market (Choices A and B). In this scenario, the justified forward P/E ratio of 4 is less than the forward P/E ratio of 5,
indicating that the stock is overvalued.
The difference in the two P/Es can be explained by assumptions for the required rate of return or the growth rate used to determine intrinsic value.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.08 Equity Valuation Concepts And Basic Tools - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 6.08 Equity Valuation Concepts And Basic Tools
question_en: Which of the following least likely requires a future long-term growth rate for valuation purposes?
explanation_en:
Analysts use valuation models to estimate the intrinsic value of a stock to determine whether it is valued fairly. Common forms of valuation models
include multiplier, present value, and asset based.
With an asset-based valuation model, a firm's estimated equity value (ie, value to shareholders) is assumed to be equal to the current fair value
of assets minus the fair value of liabilities. Analysts often start with the book values of line items on the balance sheet and make fair value
adjustments to derive their market values. Since all inputs are based on current data, no long-term growth rate (g) is needed; g is used as an
input for forecasting future cash flows (eg, dividends, free cash flows).
(Choice A) When a multiplier model is justified (ie, justified P/E), it typically is derived from a present value model (eg, discounted free cash flow,
dividend discount model), that includes g as an input.
(Choice B) Present value models (eg, dividend discount model) typically require g for forecasting a company's future financial results (eg,
dividends, free cash flows). Once forecasts are made, they are discounted to the present at an appropriate discount rate (eg, WACC) to derive an
intrinsic value.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.08 Equity Valuation Concepts And Basic Tools - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 6.08 Equity Valuation Concepts And Basic Tools
question_en: An advantage of using a present value model to value a publicly traded company's common stock is most likely that there are:
option_b: readily available values for company assets.
option_c: models to estimate the company's cost of equity capital.
explanation_en:
Present value models estimate value from the projected future cash flows that benefit common shareholders. These models use either cash
dividends or free cash flow to equity. The estimated intrinsic (ie, fundamental) value is the present value of the appropriate cash flow stream
discounted by the company's cost of equity capital. The cost of equity capital can be estimated by calculating the required rate of return using
other models (eg, CAPM).
(Choice A) Multiplier models estimate value by comparing the chosen multiple (eg, P/E, EV / EBITDA) for the company being evaluated to a
comparable company or benchmark. Finding appropriate comparables is often difficult, but present value models do not use comparable
companies to estimate intrinsic value.
(Choice B) Asset-based valuation models require estimating the fair value of company assets and liabilities. Since many operating assets are
unique to the company and trade infrequently, accurate asset values can be difficult to estimate. However, present value models do not use
company asset values to estimate the intrinsic value.

question_en: The Gordon growth model is most appropriate for a:
option_a: mature utility company with steadily increasing earnings.
option_b: firm reinvesting earnings and not currently paying a dividend.
option_c: company with earnings growth greater than the required rate of return.
explanation_en:
The Gordon growth model (GGM) is the dividend discount model that assumes the company has steady growth in earnings and a constant
dividend payout ratio, resulting in a constant dividend growth rate. The GGM is therefore appropriate for the valuation of stocks of companies
in a mature growth stage.
Under GGM assumptions, the dividend growth rate must be less than the required rate of return. If the growth rate is greater than the required
rate of return, another equity valuation model is more appropriate and the GGM should not be used. The GGM is suitable only if dividends are
considered a good indicator of company growth prospects. Dividend growth is assumed to be constant and perpetual. The required rate of return
must be known and is assumed constant.
(Choice B) The GGM uses dividends as inputs. If a firm is either not paying dividends or the dividends paid are not a good indicator of actual firm
growth, the GGM cannot be used. For example, if the dividend payout ratio is changing year to year so that the dividend growth rate does not
accurately reflect growth of earnings, then the GGM is not appropriate.
(Choice C) The GGM assumes the growth rate is less than the required rate of return. If the growth rate is greater than the required rate of
return, the GGM is not appropriate.
